The Gospel of John is the final of the four canonical Gospels in the New Testament, traditionally attributed to John the Apostle. Written likely in the late first century, it differs dramatically from the synoptic Gospels—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—in theology, narrative structure, and emphasis. It presents Jesus as the divine Logos, or Word, through lengthy philosophical discourses, mystical imagery, and symbolic miracles. Written in Greek, likely between 90 and 110 CE, decades after Jesus's death, scholars debate whether John the Apostle authored it or whether it reflects his tradition filtered through later theological reflection. The opening declares Jesus as the divine Logos with the phrase "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God," establishing his pre-incarnate divinity from the outset. John emphasizes mysticism and symbolic theology more than the synoptic Gospels, using I am statements like "I am the bread of life," "I am the light of the world," and "I am the resurrection and the life" to reveal Jesus's divine identity. It contains no nativity narrative or genealogy, instead opening with John the Baptist's testimony and focusing on extended scenes and discourses rather than rapid-fire parables. John records seven symbolic signs, or miracles: water turned to wine at Cana, healing the royal official's son, the pool of Bethesda healing, feeding five thousand, walking on water, healing the blind man, and most dramatically, raising Lazarus from the dead after four days. John uniquely details Lazarus's resurrection, the conspiracy against Lazarus that followed, and the anointing of Jesus's feet by Mary, possibly Mary Magdalene, shortly before crucifixion. It records Jesus's extended farewell discourse to the apostles and the High Priestly Prayer, emphasizing eternal life and unity with God. John also depicts Mary Magdalene as the first witness to the risen Jesus, a profound theologically significant role that elevated women's spiritual authority in early Christianity.
